title: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains
content:
Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.
“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.
His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says.
Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.
“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.
More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says.
The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.
“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement.

report.summary: UK's FCA says Meta refused joint sandbox testing of its Muse AI assistant, as regulators warn Meta must ensure consumer-law compliance.
report.background: Meta launched Muse, a personal AI assistant, in North America in September and has already surpassed 10 million users. The tool is designed to act on users' behalf, including shopping and potentially payments, making it part of a broader wave of agentic AI products entering the UK market. UK regulators—the Financial Conduct Authority, Competition and Markets Authority, and Information Commissioner's Office—are scrutinising how such agents interact with consumers, handle personal data, and execute transactions. The FCA hoped to joint-test Muse in its regulatory sandbox, but Meta declined the suggestion. The episode highlights growing tension between fast-moving AI agent rollouts and regulators' desire for pre-deployment visibility, especially as British retailers work with Meta to prepare for Muse's UK arrival.
key_points: The FCA invited Meta to jointly test Muse in its regulatory sandbox, but Meta declined. Colin Payne, the FCA's head of innovation, said the request was reasonable because regulators want to see how an autonomous assistant would interact with ordinary customers before broad UK rollout.

Payne is especially focused on payments and unintended prompt consequences. Several UK retailers, including Sainsbury's, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group, and Currys, have worked with Meta on Muse access, raising questions about how agents will transact and whether consumers understand the risks.

Timing is a friction point. Payne said sandbox testing normally takes weeks or months to plan, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month. Meta says it has engaged constructively with regulators and will continue to do so.

Other UK watchdogs are also circling. The ICO stressed that users must understand and control how Muse uses their data, while the CMA has already required Meta to adjust UK terms to promise reasonable skill and care, even as the terms acknowledge outputs may be inaccurate.

Scale is driving scrutiny. Muse has more than 10 million North American users, and UK regulators expect significant uptake because Brits already use Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. The CMA says it will not hesitate to act if concerns arise.
report.impact: The standoff signals that agentic AI is entering a tougher regulatory phase. For the AI industry, Meta's refusal may invite closer scrutiny and set an early precedent that pre-deployment sandbox testing is expected for consumer-facing agents that can spend money or act autonomously. Developers building shopping, payment, or personal-assistant agents should prioritise auditability, user consent, transaction limits, and clear error handling. For regular users, Muse-style assistants may make shopping and tasks more convenient, but the FCA's concerns underscore risks: opaque prompts, mistaken purchases, and unclear liability. Regulators are likely to demand clearer disclosures and controls, potentially slowing UK launches while raising compliance costs for companies deploying autonomous agents.
report.tools: For teams building or testing agentic assistants, watch open-source and developer tools such as Promptfoo for prompt/regression testing, Langfuse and AgentOps for agent observability, OpenAI Evals for model evaluations, and Guardrails AI for runtime safety checks. Also follow FCA sandbox guidance, CMA consumer-protection statements, and ICO data-protection guidance for AI agents, as these will shape UK compliance expectations for autonomous shopping and payment tools.
